stories.topic: The One Time Amit Smoked Up — With a World-Famous Guitarist
stories.summary: Amit recalls smoking marijuana exactly once, around 1995, in a car with his friend Amit Saigal and 'a world famous guitarist I won't name because it'll seem like too much of a humble brag.' He was in his early twenties, sitting in the back seat. They asked him if he wanted to try; he did. He felt nothing.
stories.insight: A small, disarming admission that lets him discuss recreational drugs from a place of personal honesty rather than abstraction. The 'felt nothing' detail is the joke and the point: a one-shot moral panic about marijuana sits poorly with the lived experience of millions.

stories.topic: The Matunga Racket — How the Police Extorted Gay Men
stories.summary: Around 2007-08, before Grindr or Tinder, gay men in Bombay used classified websites to find each other. Vikram Doctor pointed Amit to a racket the police were running: a cop would pose as a man looking for love, fix a meeting at Matunga station, and when the target showed up he'd be 'nabbed' and extorted under threat of being outed to family. In some cases the cops would walk the victim to an ATM and empty his account on the spot.
stories.insight: A vivid illustration of how outlawing a victimless act doesn't just chill behaviour — it weaponises a primal social shame and hands it to whoever holds state power. The bad cop is downstream of the bad law; the incentive structure manufactures the predator.

stories.topic: Match-Fixing as a Symptom of Banned Betting
stories.summary: Drawing on years as a cricket journalist, Amit pushes back on the routine conflation of betting and match-fixing. Match-fixing happens precisely because betting is illegal — the underworld captures the activity, money flows escape the regulator's gaze, and the people running the books have every reason to corrupt the on-field result. Today it's likely lower than before because players are paid more (incentives have shifted), but the underlying logic remains.
stories.insight: When you push a popular activity underground, you don't just get a black market in that activity — you get every adjacent crime its operators can monetise. Match-fixing is the externality of betting prohibition, not an argument for it.

stories.topic: Aella — Sex Worker, Data Scientist, $100 Newsletter
stories.summary: Amit cites Aella as one of his favourite Twitter accounts: a sex worker who runs large-scale surveys and writes incisively about gender relations, openly discussed organising a gangbang for her own birthday. Her newsletter is one of the few Amit pays $100 a year for, because of how 'packed with insight' it is.
stories.insight: A real human counter to the reflexive Indian image of prostitution as coercion-soaked tragedy. Agency, intellect and sex work can coexist; the case for legalisation begins with seeing that they do.

stories.topic: The Cannibal of Rotenburg — Armin Meiwes and Bernd Brandes
stories.summary: In 2003, a 42-year-old German named Armin Meiwes advertised online for a well-built young man who wanted to be eaten. Bernd Brandes responded, travelled to meet him, and at every stage — captured on camera — consented. Brandes took 20 sleeping pills and a bottle of schnapps; Meiwes severed Brandes' penis and the two ate it together; Meiwes then read a Star Trek novel while Brandes showered, eventually killed him with a cleaver, froze the body, and consumed it over many days with olive oil and garlic. Cannibalism is not a crime in Germany.
stories.insight: The case is built precisely to break the harm-principle calculator: rights infringement is unclear, consent is documented, and yet every moral instinct screams 'crime.' That gap — between intuition and principle — is what icky problems exist to expose.

stories.summary: Amit revisits two classic 'icky' problems from the ethics literature. One: you've bought a chicken to kill and eat; before killing it you have sex with it — is this wrong? Two: an adult brother and sister, using contraception so no children are produced, choose to have sex with each other — is this wrong? Instinct shouts yes; rational analysis on harm-principle grounds finds no answer.
stories.insight: Our moral intuitions are the residue of prehistoric programming we don't fully understand. That's reason enough to be wary of any state — or dominant social group — that converts disgust directly into law.

stories.topic: 1 in 20 Death Row Inmates Was Innocent — In the First World
stories.summary: Ajay cites a striking finding: roughly 5% of people executed by the state in advanced economies are later believed to have been innocent. This is at the highest evidentiary bar in the highest-capacity criminal-justice systems on earth. From there he asks the obvious follow-up: what is the equivalent failure rate of the Indian state, with its weaker capacity?
stories.insight: Calibrate your trust in convictions to the system that produced them. If even the best state-machinery puts an innocent person on death row 5% of the time, the prior on a random Indian conviction being a miscarriage of justice is high — which is itself an argument for keeping the criminal code narrow.

stories.summary: Ajay traces a clean causal arrow: import duties created smuggling; smuggling rewarded scale; scale gave rise to organisational capability in crime. The Haji Mastan empires were not freaks of nature — they were the predictable response to the licence-permit-raj's incentive structure. Once the organisation exists, it doesn't stay confined to the original prohibition.
stories.insight: Banning victimless activity doesn't just produce 'more crime' — it incubates organisational capability that scales across crimes. Better, where you cannot avoid criminality, to leave it to lone rangers than to fund the building of firms.

stories.topic: Alan Turing — Hero, Dreamer, Casualty of a Bad Law
stories.summary: Ajay closes the episode by recommending Alan Turing as a person to study. Turing helped crack the German Enigma — a turning point of WWII — and conceived of the computer before there were computers. His life was destroyed by old British laws criminalising homosexuality. He was chemically castrated and is widely believed to have killed himself.
stories.insight: When the state criminalises a victimless private act, the cost isn't only the daily indignity it imposes on millions — it is also the exceptional lives it cuts short. Turing is a single name that stands for an enormous, mostly invisible loss.

stories.topic: Liver Doctor on Why Even Occasional Alcohol Is Bad
stories.summary: Amit references his Seen and Unseen episode with hepatologist Abby Phillips. Common defence: 'a glass of wine is good for the heart.' Phillips' reply: even if true, the damage to the liver outweighs the cardiovascular benefit, so the right move is to abstain. Amit himself drinks once or twice a year, mostly with friends on a hot summer day; Ajay has never had alcohol in his life.
stories.insight: The personal honesty matters precisely because the policy argument is libertarian: 'I think alcohol is bad and I avoid it' coexists cleanly with 'and the state has no business imposing my view on you.' The case against prohibition does not require pretending the substance is benign.

recommendations.item: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2008 column laying out the case the episode unpacks at length.
recommendations.reason: The original written form of the argument — useful both as a primer and as proof that the position long predates this episode.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2017 essay in Pragati on policing morality.
recommendations.reason: A companion piece to the victimless-crimes argument, focused on why public moral panics keep producing bad law.

recommendations.item: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Phillips
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive with hepatologist Abby Phillips.
recommendations.reason: Source of the claim that even an occasional drink does net liver damage that outweighs supposed cardiovascular benefits — useful evidence that the case against prohibition does not depend on pretending alcohol is harmless.

recommendations.item: Bootleggers and Baptists — The Education of a Regulatory Economist
recommendations.creator: Bruce Yandle
recommendations.context: Yandle's classic essay on the unholy alliance between moral campaigners and the underworld they unwittingly enrich.
recommendations.reason: The conceptual spine of the prohibition chapter: the Baptist supplies the moral cover, the bootlegger supplies the alcohol, and their incentives are aligned even when they appear opposed. Amit notes the film Raees got the dynamic exactly backwards.

recommendations.item: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's takedown of the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees.
recommendations.reason: The film stages the Baptist and the bootlegger as enemies; in reality their incentives align. Amit's review uses Yandle's lens to explain why the film's moral architecture collapses.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the history of dietary guidelines and the sugar lobby.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 1977 US dietary-guidelines story — sugar absolved, fat demonised, obesity epidemic ignited — invoked here as a parable for why the state should not be a nutritional authority.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2010 column arguing every life decision is a probability bet.
recommendations.reason: The basis for destigmatising gambling: marriage, jobs, housing, parenting — all are bets weighed against probabilities. Singling out games of chance for prohibition is intellectually incoherent.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.reason: Develops the argument that match-fixing is the externality of betting prohibition — bring betting overground through respectable institutions and the on-field corruption mostly evaporates.

recommendations.creator: Aella
recommendations.context: Twitter account of the sex worker, surveyor and writer.
recommendations.reason: A live counter-image to the standard Indian script for prostitution: agency, intellect and sex work can coexist openly. Amit cites her surveys as 'incredible' on data about gender relations.

recommendations.creator: Aella
recommendations.reason: One of the very few newsletters Amit pays $100 a year for — 'so packed with insight about gender relations.'

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's mid-2000s Mint column on a Bombay police extortion ring against gay men.
recommendations.reason: The case study at the heart of the homosexuality chapter: outlawing a victimless act creates a primal shame that the state then monetises. The bad cop is a downstream artefact of the bad law.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode on liberty and economic growth.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pointer for listeners who want to take seriously the claim that 8% GDP growth is the most powerful instrument for women's emancipation in India.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode on the practical mechanics of economic development.
recommendations.reason: The companion to Why Freedom Matters: if you actually care about marginalised groups, the levers that work are growth and institution-building, not moralising bans.

recommendations.item: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen and Unseen episode on novel metrics for women's empowerment.
recommendations.reason: Amit's own provocation in that episode: rising divorce rates are a positive metric, because they signal women acquiring the financial and social ability to walk out of bad marriages.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.reason: Crystallises the argument that high divorce rates are a feminist victory — and that no-fault divorce is a more effective lever for protecting battered wives than alcohol prohibition could ever be.

recommendations.creator: various biographers
recommendations.context: Ajay's closing recommendation: study the life of Alan Turing, war hero and pioneer theoretical computer scientist destroyed by British anti-homosexuality law.
recommendations.reason: Engaging with Turing's story should 'reshape your moral calculus' — both the daily indignity of bad law and the exceptional lives it cuts short become viscerally legible.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'state capability is a finite budget' frame Ajay uses in the closing chapter: India's tinsy-vinsy reservoir of state capacity should be spent on a few primordial problems, not splurged on policing private behaviour.

core_ideas.explanation: A crime, in the principled sense, is the infringement of someone's rights — most fundamentally the right to self-ownership and its derivatives (life, property, free speech). 'Whatever the law says is illegal' and 'what is actually wrong' are not the same set. The state's only legitimate role is to prevent rights infringements, not to engineer society or enforce a moral aesthetic.
core_ideas.quote: If there is a crime, there must be a victim.

core_ideas.concept: Three Objections to Banning Victimless Crimes
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's structured case has three legs. (1) Moral: consenting adults' voluntary interactions in the bedroom, marketplace or public square are simply not the state's business. (2) Practical: prohibition does not extinguish demand; it births an underworld that brings coercion, fraud, low quality, and adjacent crimes. (3) Power: the state already has a monopoly on coercion; granting it arbitrary licence to refashion society is dangerous because the people you hate most could be in power tomorrow, applying the same tool to their values.
core_ideas.quote: A person you hate most in the world could be in power tomorrow and they'll pass laws according to their values.

core_ideas.explanation: Economists measure prohibition's success by the black-market price premium — the larger the premium, the more 'effective' the enforcement. But the same premium signals to criminal entrepreneurs that the prize for entry is enormous. So short-run enforcement success directly stokes long-run organisational scaling of the underworld. The very metric by which the state wins is the metric that ensures it loses.
core_ideas.quote: On one hand, the measure of successful enforcement is that the price of the forbidden substances should be high. But that very fact… sets off greater energy by private people to engage in entry strategies.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay distinguishes two regimes of crime: solo creators (a lone con artist, a thief) and firms (Haji Mastan-scale operations with hierarchies, complexity and capability). Prohibition is dangerous in part because it doesn't merely create more crime — it incubates organisational capability that, once built, scales horizontally across crimes. Better the lone ranger than the firm.
core_ideas.quote: It is better for us to have lone rangers and solo creators in the world of crime.

core_ideas.explanation: Bruce Yandle's frame: every prohibition has a Baptist (the moral campaigner with high-minded reasons) and a bootlegger (the underworld supplier who profits from the ban). Their incentives are aligned even when they appear opposed — both want the prohibition to stay. Amit notes the film Raees stages them as enemies; in reality they are tacit allies. Apply the lens widely: behind any moral panic, look for the bootlegger.

The recurring formula across alcohol, drugs, gambling, prostitution: legalise, bring overground, regulate with a light touch, let respectable institutions enter. Sunlight makes regulation possible — it lets you see the money flows, the worker conditions, the quality. Prohibition forecloses the basic precondition of regulation: visibility. Imagine an HDFC-style account for cricket betting; imagine brothels with codified worker rights. The point is not that those institutions are perfect but that they are addressable.

Locke's foundational right is self-ownership: I am not the property of the state or anyone else; I am my own property. Every other liberal right — life, free speech, property — derives from it. The implication is uncomfortable: the right to life includes the right to end one's own life. Suicide and euthanasia, on this view, are exercises of self-ownership, not crimes against the state.

Suicide, in much of recent Indian history, was the one crime you got punished for failing to commit. As a social problem, it demands compassion, mental-health infrastructure, and friends who notice. As a legal problem, it is incoherent: if I own myself, my reasons for ending my life are no business of the state. Euthanasia is the structured edge case — clearly desirable in principle, dangerous to deploy in low-state-capacity settings where it could be weaponised by relatives against the elderly.

core_ideas.concept: Free Speech Absolutism and the Direct-Incitement Carve-Out
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's free-speech position: speech becomes punishable only when it directly incites a specific harm — 'jaake Amit ko maaro' is wrong because the maaro-ing is the actual crime. Otherwise, even hate speech should remain legal. The reason is empirical, not aesthetic: laws against hate speech will always be used against free speech. India's Sections 295A and 153A are putatively about preventing communal violence; in practice they are weapons for arresting dissenters. The intent is irrelevant; the incentive is everything.
core_ideas.quote: Laws against hate speech will always be used against free speech.

core_ideas.explanation: Some moral intuitions resist rationalisation. Sex with the chicken you're about to kill and eat; consenting siblings using contraception. Both feel obviously wrong; neither survives a harm-principle audit. Our intuitions are the residue of prehistoric programming whose purposes we don't understand. That alone should make us suspicious of converting moral disgust into law — both in the hands of the state and the dominant social group of the moment.

core_ideas.concept: The Cannibal Test for the Harm Principle
core_ideas.explanation: The Meiwes-Brandes case is engineered to break naive harm-principle thinking. Consent is documented at every step; cannibalism is not illegal in Germany. So is it murder? If you say Brandes was mentally ill and incapable of consenting, you must extend the same charity to Meiwes ('no sane person would do this') and reach for an insanity defence. Either you swallow a deeply repugnant outcome on rationalist grounds, or you concede that some moral intuitions are doing legitimate work that pure consent-talk cannot capture. The point is to live with the tension, not resolve it cheaply.

core_ideas.concept: State Capability as a Finite Budget
core_ideas.explanation: From Kelkar and Shah: state capability in India is not large; it is tinsy-vinsy. Treat it as a scarce resource. The wise strategy is to focus that thin capability on a few primordial functions — defence, criminal justice, monetary policy, financial regulation, tax administration — and accept that everything else is best left unregulated. Sweden can splurge state capability on lifestyle policing. India cannot. We have a 50-100 year journey to merely build the basics; squandering capacity on victimless crimes is a category error.
core_ideas.quote: We face a fifty or a hundred year journey to learning how to do… state capability emerges very slowly.

core_ideas.explanation: Roughly 1 in 20 people executed in advanced economies is later believed to have been innocent. This is at the highest evidentiary bar in the highest-capacity state machineries on earth. Calibrate your priors accordingly: any conviction in a lower-capacity system carries a much higher chance of being a miscarriage of justice. Skepticism toward the state's instrument of force is not contrarianism — it is the empirically warranted default.

core_ideas.concept: Means-Ends Thinking — and Why No-Fault Divorce Beats Prohibition
core_ideas.explanation: If you genuinely care about battered wives, the moralistic lever (ban alcohol, jail drunk husbands) is the worst tool you have. The effective lever is power: make divorce easy, frictionless, and codified — split jointly created wealth at separation, no questions asked. A woman who can walk away changes her husband's incentives directly. This is what means-ends thinking looks like: pick the lever rooted in the humanities and social sciences, not the lever that maximises emotional outrage.
core_ideas.quote: Just an emotional outrage is the surest way of getting to a wrong answer.

core_ideas.explanation: The single most powerful instrument for the emancipation and status of women in India is 8% GDP growth. Empowerment is downstream of economic capability — the ability to support oneself, walk away from a bad marriage, refuse a bad job. This generalises beyond women: every marginalised group is best served by the growth project. Bleeding-heart moralism without a growth strategy is sentiment dressed up as ethics.
core_ideas.quote: If you care about women in India, you should sign up for the growth project.

core_ideas.concept: Rising Divorce Rates as a Positive Metric
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's contrarian metric for women's empowerment: rising divorce rates. The frame inverts the conservative reading. A society where divorces go up is a society where more women have the financial and social ability to walk out of bad marriages. Reagan's no-fault divorce reform — much hated by the traditional right — was one of the great quiet feminist victories of 20th-century America.

core_ideas.concept: These Are Not Crimes At All
core_ideas.explanation: The closing reframing: don't even concede the linguistic ground. Alcohol, drugs, gambling, prostitution, homosexuality, self-harm, hate speech — calling these 'victimless crimes' is itself a concession. They are not crimes that happen to lack victims; they are not crimes. The argument is not 'the state should deprioritise these crimes' but 'the state should recognise these are outside its purview entirely.'
core_ideas.quote: These are not crimes. Therefore kindly stay away.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on his 1995 marijuana experiment with a 'world famous guitarist I won't name because it'll seem like too much of a humble brag' — and the punchline that he 'felt nothing.'

Amit on the bureaucratic absurdity of import duties: 'I buy something in America, I bring it here and I sell it to a friend. And immediately it is a crime because I haven't paid the haftaa to the state.'

Amit, on his Bombay police bias: 'I've seen the Bombay police up close and no other police, and they're super efficient and they're good citizens.' (Said while explaining how the same force runs the Matunga racket.)

Ajay's pitch for the episode: 'I'd sell to moms — please think and understand this landscape so you can talk to your kids.' (The author of the most rigorous case for legal cocaine, marketing himself as the friend of mothers.)
Amit on the gourmet cannibalism detail: '[Meiwes] eventually ate it with olive oil and garlic. I don't know why there was no salt — perhaps human flesh has natural salt like bacon does.'

Amit on Star Trek as a cannibal's reading material: while Brandes showered after his self-amputation, Meiwes 'sat and read a Star Trek novel.' The detail lands the icky horror harder than any speech could.

Amit on the chicken thought experiment: pose the question of whether having sex with a chicken before killing and eating it is wrong, and 'the why has no answer because rationally it is not wrong but our moral instincts take us in another direction.'
Amit on imagining mainstream finance taking on prostitution: 'I don't think HDFC or IDFC will do it, but you get what I'm saying.'
Amit on the 'whore' insult: 'Like, which of us is not a whore in some way or the other, if you use the term in that manner?'

Amit on how the Twitter rant against Reagan converted him: someone listed 'five things Ronald Reagan got wrong,' and as Amit read through them he realised Reagan got all of them right — including no-fault divorce.
Ajay's diagnosis of Indian state capability: 'tinsy-vinsy.' (The technical term.)
Amit on suicide's old legal status: 'It was the one crime for which you got punished if you failed to commit it.'
John Stuart Mill's Harm Principle — invoked throughout, though never named: individuals should be free to do whatever they wish, so long as they do not harm others.
John Locke on self-ownership — the foundational right from which all other liberal rights are derived in Amit's framing.
Bruce Yandle's 'Bootleggers and Baptists' — the regulatory-economist parable that powers the prohibition chapter.
Henry David Thoreau's 'lives of quiet desperation' — borrowed to describe the closeted homosexual under criminalising laws.
Sections 295A and 153A of the Indian Penal Code — the putatively-anti-hate-speech laws Amit cites as the textbook case of how such statutes are weaponised against dissenters.

The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, India — defines prostitution as 'sexual exploitation or abuse of persons for commercial purposes,' bizarrely conflating the act with the coercion that may surround it. Compare the Oxford definition: 'engaging in sexual activity with someone for payment.'

Article 377 of the Indian Penal Code — the colonial-era statute that criminalised homosexuality in India until the 2018 Navtej Singh Johar verdict. (Amit refers to it twice in passing as 'Article 370,' but the substance and the timeline place it squarely as 377.)

The 1977 US Dietary Guidelines — the inflection point at which sugar was absolved and fat demonised, kicking off the obesity epidemic. Cited as a parable of state nutritional intervention going wrong.
Haji Mastan — the smuggler-don whose empire is invoked as the canonical example of how prohibition (here, of imports) builds organisational capability in the underworld.
Armin Meiwes, the Cannibal of Rotenburg, and his victim Bernd Brandes (2001) — the real-world case used as the central thought experiment in the chapter on moral intuition and consent.
